planting.note: Mount on untreated bark, driftwood, or a shaded tree branch in dappled light; needs no soil. Native from Mexico to Costa Rica with historic records in the lower Rio Grande valley of South Texas and the Florida Keys, it clumps readily and is best sited in a protected zone 9b-11 spot outdoors.

directions: Tillandsia schiedeana is a clump-forming epiphyte native from Mexico south through Guatemala and Honduras to Costa Rica, with historic collections also recorded from the lower Rio Grande valley of South Texas and the Florida Keys. It forms an upright rosette of narrow, silvery-gray, slightly recurved leaves that readily produce basal offsets, forming dense mats on a host branch within a few seasons. In summer, a branched, red-bracted inflorescence rises above the foliage bearing small tubular yellow flowers. Mount on untreated bark or driftwood in dappled light with no soil, and water by misting or dunking two to three times weekly in the growing season, tapering off in winter to avoid rot in cool, damp conditions.

planting.note: Secure offsets to the rough bark of a buttonwood, mangrove, or oak branch in bright, humid, partial shade; needs no soil and no cold tolerance, so is only reliable in frost-free zone 10-11 sites. Listed as endangered in Florida due to habitat loss and the introduced Mexican bromeliad weevil.

directions: Tillandsia flexuosa, the twisted airplant, ranges throughout the Caribbean and continental tropical America and reaches its northern limit in the mangrove edges and tropical hardwood hammocks of the Florida Keys, where it is listed as endangered. Its thick, gray-green leaves develop characteristic reddish-brown cross-banding and twist and curl with age, distinguishing it from Florida's other wild-pine tillandsias. A tall, branched inflorescence of orange-red bracts and violet tubular flowers rises well above the foliage in summer, and like Tillandsia fasciculata it has suffered steep population declines from the introduced Mexican bromeliad weevil. Secure offsets to the rough bark of a buttonwood, mangrove, or oak branch in bright, humid, partial shade and mist regularly, since this species needs consistently warm, frost-free conditions.

planting.note: Mount on a sturdy tree or large piece of driftwood, or grow in a large well-drained container, in bright filtered light; this large species has no frost tolerance and needs zone 10-12 outdoor conditions. Keep the central tank filled with fresh water and flush periodically to prevent stagnation.

directions: Aechmea bracteata is a large, architectural epiphyte native to the Gulf lowlands of Mexico, the Yucatan Peninsula, and Central America, where it grows high in the canopy on oaks and other hardwoods. Its broad, gray-green, spine-edged leaves form a substantial tank-type rosette two feet or more across, and a tall, upright inflorescence of overlapping orange-red bracts opens to reveal small yellow flowers followed by blue-black berries. Because of its size and weight at maturity, it is best grown mounted on a sturdy tree or large piece of driftwood, or in a large well-drained container, in bright filtered light with no true cold tolerance. Keep the central tank filled with fresh water and flush periodically; established plants are drought-tolerant once mounted and make a bold specimen in a south Florida or similarly frost-free tree canopy.

planting.note: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in well-draining soil or a container in protected zone 9b-11 sites; spreads by offsets into informal colonies. Keep the central cup topped with water.

directions: Billbergia decora is native to montane and foothill forests of Peru and Bolivia, where it grows as an epiphyte or terrestrial clump-former in the dappled light of the forest understory. It forms loose, tubular rosettes of soft gray-green, powdery leaves that spread readily by offsets into informal colonies. In late winter or spring, an arching, pendant flower stalk emerges bearing rose-pink bracts and tubular green petals edged in blue, a display similar to its better-known relative Billbergia nutans but on a slightly more compact plant. Grow in partial shade to filtered sun with the central cup kept filled with water, and expect it to tolerate brief cool spells once established outdoors in protected zone 9b-11 gardens.
